title: Configuration providers (JSON, environment variables, command line)
hook: Configuration providers are the plug-in sources that feed key-value settings into your Web API — JSON files, environment variables, and command-line arguments are the three you will use on every project.

blocks.text: A configuration provider is a class that implements IConfigurationProvider and contributes key-value pairs to the merged IConfiguration tree. WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args) registers a default chain: appsettings.json, appsettings.{Environment}.json, user secrets (Development only), environment variables, and command-line arguments. Later providers override earlier ones for the same key. Keys use colon notation (Section:SubSection:Key) regardless of which provider supplied them.

entries.plainDefinition: Read-only view of merged settings from all providers. Use GetSection, indexer, or Get<T> to read values.
Loads data into the configuration dictionary. JSON, environment variables, and Azure Key Vault each have a provider.
Fluent API to add providers before the host is built. Host builder calls this internally.
Wraps another IConfiguration as a provider — useful for tests or importing a subset.

blocks.text: Every Web API setting — connection strings, JWT issuer URLs, Redis endpoints, feature toggles — flows through providers. Misunderstanding override order causes staging credentials in production or secrets committed to git. Kubernetes and Docker inject environment variables; local dev uses JSON and user secrets. Senior interviews expect you to explain which provider wins when the same key appears in appsettings.json and an environment variable.

blocks.title: Last provider wins
blocks.body: Default order: appsettings.json → appsettings.{Environment}.json → user secrets (Development) → environment variables → command line. Later sources override earlier ones for the same key path.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Host builder creates ConfigurationManager
items.body: WebApplication.CreateBuilder registers default sources in a fixed order.

items.title: Each provider loads data
items.body: JsonConfigurationProvider parses files; EnvironmentVariablesConfigurationProvider reads OS env vars with double-underscore mapping.

items.title: Keys merge into flat dictionary
items.body: Nested JSON becomes Section:Sub:Key. All providers contribute to one IConfigurationRoot.

items.title: ReloadOnChange providers subscribe
items.body: JSON providers with reloadOnChange: true watch file changes and raise IChangeToken for hot reload.

snippet.label: Default host configuration (implicit)
snippet.explanation: CreateBuilder wires the standard chain. Indexer returns string or null. GetValue<T> parses with a default fallback when the key is missing.

snippet.label: Add a custom JSON provider
snippet.explanation: AddJsonFile after CreateBuilder appends providers — they override earlier keys. reloadOnChange enables file watcher hot reload. IConfigurationRoot.Providers lists the chain for troubleshooting.

snippet.label: Environment variable naming convention
snippet.explanation: Environment variables cannot contain colons on all platforms. Double underscore maps to hierarchical keys. This is how Kubernetes secrets and Docker -e flags override appsettings in production.

snippet.label: Command-line overrides for local debugging
snippet.explanation: Command-line args use colon keys like JSON. Registered last in the default chain so they override everything — handy for one-off local runs without editing files.

blocks.title: Configuration sources in Node vs ASP.NET Core
Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using single underscore in env vars (ConnectionStrings_OrdersDb) — must be double underscore. Adding AddEnvironmentVariables before JSON manually and expecting JSON to override env vars. Forgetting optional: true on environment-specific JSON so missing Staging file crashes startup. Reading IConfiguration in singleton services at construction time instead of using IOptionsMonitor for reloadable values.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: log the resolved configuration source when a setting looks wrong — IConfigurationRoot.GetDebugView() dumps the full key tree with provider origins in Development. In Kubernetes, describe a pod and verify env vars use double-underscore naming. Application Insights custom events on startup can record non-secret config fingerprints (provider count, environment name). When a setting does not reload, check whether the provider implements reload (JSON with reloadOnChange) versus one-shot providers (environment variables are read once at startup unless you rebuild configuration).

blocks.title: Provider tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Typos in __ naming; no hot reload by default
Not available in container ENTRYPOINT without passing args
Startup latency if not using managed identity cache

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying environment variables and JSON merge with 'JSON always wins' — last provider wins, and env vars typically override JSON. Not knowing the double-underscore convention. Claiming all providers support hot reload. Unable to name the default provider order from WebApplication.CreateBuilder.

interviewTakeaways: Configuration providers are pluggable sources that merge into IConfiguration; later providers override earlier keys.
Default chain: appsettings.json → appsettings.{Environment}.json → user secrets → environment variables → command line.
Production tip: Kubernetes secrets map to env vars with double underscore (ConnectionStrings__OrdersDb); verify with kubectl describe pod.
60s: Providers merge key-value pairs. Last wins. Env vars use __ for :. CreateBuilder registers JSON, env, CLI. IConfigurationRoot lists providers for debugging.
Follow-up: which providers support reloadOnChange and how does that connect to IOptionsMonitor?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'JSON overrides environment variables' gets you rejected — env vars and command line come later and win.
Single underscore in env var names (Section_Key) — must be double underscore (Section__Key).
Strong answer: 'Last provider wins. Env vars use __ mapping. I use GetDebugView in dev and kubectl env inspection in prod to trace overrides.'
introducedIn: ASP.NET Core 1.0 configuration abstractions; unified in .NET Core 2.0+

jsTsCorrelations.note: Node apps often load .env then override with process.env manually. ASP.NET Core builds the merge order into the host — no dotenv package needed; env vars are a first-class provider.
NestJS ConfigModule loads .env and JSON with explicit load order. ASP.NET Core's host builder registers the same idea by default — env vars and CLI args override files without extra wiring.
